theory.overview: Input/Output systems handle communication between programs and the external world. From blocking I/O to async/await and event loops, modern systems employ sophisticated techniques to handle thousands of concurrent connections efficiently. Understanding I/O models helps you build high-performance networked applications.

keyConcepts.title: Blocking vs Non-blocking I/O
keyConcepts.content: Blocking I/O waits until operation completes, consuming a thread. Non-blocking I/O returns immediately, requiring the program to check completion status. Async I/O uses callbacks or futures to notify completion.

keyConcepts.title: Event Loops
keyConcepts.content: Event loops (reactor pattern) use a single thread to handle many connections. They monitor file descriptors for readiness, dispatching events to handlers. This avoids thread-per-connection overhead.

keyConcepts.title: System Calls & Kernel
keyConcepts.content: I/O operations require system calls transitioning to kernel mode. select/poll/epoll (Linux) and kqueue (BSD/macOS) let a single thread monitor many file descriptors efficiently.

keyConcepts.title: Zero-Copy I/O
keyConcepts.content: Techniques like sendfile() avoid copying data through user space. The kernel transfers data directly from disk to socket, reducing CPU overhead and memory bandwidth.

steps.title: File Descriptors
steps.content: Everything is a file in Unix. File descriptors are integers representing open files, sockets, or pipes. Operations like read(), write(), close() work on all types.

steps.title: The select() Loop
steps.content: Build a set of file descriptors to monitor. select() blocks until any is ready. Iterate through descriptors to find which ones need attention and process them.

steps.title: epoll & Scalability
steps.content: epoll (Linux) scales better than select() for many connections. It uses a kernel-side data structure and notifies only ready descriptors, avoiding O(n) scans.

practiceProblems.title: Event Loop Order
practiceProblems.description: In an event loop, if fd1 and fd2 are both ready, which is processed first?
practiceProblems.solution: Depends on implementation. Typically the one with lower fd number or the one that was registered first. Order shouldn't matter for correctness.

practiceProblems.title: C10K Problem
practiceProblems.description: Why can't thread-per-connection handle 10,000 concurrent connections?
practiceProblems.solution: Thread stacks consume memory (~8MB each = 80GB). Context switching overhead becomes significant. Thread creation/destruction is expensive.
